newsitem.title: USA: CSX, Norfolk Southern near terms on Conrail split.
newsitem.headline: CSX, Norfolk Southern near terms on Conrail split.

text.p: CSX Corp. and Norfolk Southern Corp. are expected next week to unveil plans for their $10.3 billion acquisition of Conrail Inc. that call for Norfolk Southern to acquire more than half of the Northeast railroad's assets, according to sources familiar with the companies.
The railroads had hoped to announce the specifics of the break-up this week, but the negotiations have been extremely complex and more time was needed, the sources said.
"The exact percentages are still not done, but Norfolk Southern clearly will have the majority of the economic value when it's all over," said one source, who did not want to be identified.

Under the anticipated plan that will divide Conrail's vast Northeast network, Norfolk Southern is expected to gain access to the New York/New Jersey region via the former Pennsylvania Railroad line. CSX will win access to the region via the old New York Central line running through Chicago and New York State into New York City.
"The basic route structure has been pretty well decided for a long time," the source said.
Norfolk Southern spokesman Robert Fort declined to comment on the negotiations, saying only that they were continuing. CSX also declined to comment.
The break-up of the Philadelphia-based railroad is part of a negotiated settlement struck earlier this month that ended a five-month takeover battle.
Conrail and Richmond, Va.-based CSX annnounced a friendly merger in October, but the transaction quickly was eclipsed by a hostile and higher bid from Norfolk, Va.-based Norfolk Southern.
After a bidding war and a stalemate, CSX earlier this month raised its offer to meet Norfolk Southern's bid of $115 per share and agreed to negotiate a division of assets with Norfolk Southern.
Although the stalemate ended this month, industry and Wall Street experts had increasingly anticipated that a break-up of Conrail would be the likely outcome.
Industry experts put little significance on the expectation that Norfolk Southern, once the hostile bidder, will receive the larger chunk of the prize.

"It is ironic that Norfolk Southern would get a bigger piece of Conrail, having come from behind like that, but on the other hand, if you are going to have an equitable split of Conrail, Norfolk Southern has to have a bigger piece because CSX has a bigger piece already of the eastern market. It's logical," said Anthony Hatch of NatWest Securities Corp.

Although the companies are expected to discuss route details next week, Wall Street analysts said it will likely be a few more weeks before they hear specific details from the victors about cost-cutting, revenue growth and capital spending on the new lines.

"Versus what CSX and Conrail had hoped for at the start, (the asset division) implies less downside risk and less longterm potential benefits" for CSX and Norfork Southern, said James Higgins of Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette.
Both railroads are expected to upgrade the Conrail lines and facilities to meet anticipated growth.

The stocks of CSX and Norfolk Southern declined Thursday afternoon on the New York Stock Exchange amid broader market declines. Shares of CSX fell $1.125 to $47 and Norfolk Southern lost $1.125 to $89.50.
